wine.name: Marquesa de Alorna Grande Reserva Tinto
wine.grapes: A blend of red grapes that the house does not disclose, describing it on its own pages as a secret blend.
wine.sites: The estate's own vineyards at Almeirim, on the left bank of the Tejo, which run from the fertile, flood prone Campo beside the river to the sandy, stony Charneca to the south; the house names no single parcel for this wine.
wine.making: Aged for fourteen months in new French oak barrels, by the house's own pages and a merchant's sheet, then rested in bottle at the estate for a year or two, by vintage, before release.
wine.glass: Blackberry and raspberry with a perfume of wild flowers, then chocolate, white pepper and the toast of new oak; medium to full bodied, with firm tannin, balanced acidity and a dry finish.
wine.ageing: Released after its rest in bottle and open from the start, it has the tannin and the oak to keep for some years more in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius, as the house advises; decant a young bottle an hour ahead; a large red wine glass.

records.table: Marquesa de Alorna Grande Reserva is the red flagship of Quinta da Alorna, an Almeirim estate born in 1723: a blend the house keeps secret, aged fourteen months in new French oak. Expect blackberry, chocolate and toast over firm tannin, and pour it with roast kid or game.
records.story: The estate was born in 1723, by its own account, as the Quinta de Vale de Nabais, a farm at Almeirim on the left bank of the Tejo. The house names as its founder Pedro Miguel de Almeida Portugal (1688 to 1756), Count of Assumar, who governed Portuguese India as viceroy from 1744. In 1746 his forces took the Indian fortress of Alorna, and in 1748 the king made him Marquis of Alorna; he then gave the farm the name it bears. His granddaughter Leonor de Almeida Portugal (1750 to 1839), the fourth Marquise, wrote verse as Alcipe and is remembered as a voice of Portuguese Pre-Romanticism, and the house's Grande Reserva range carries her title. Two of her daughters later sold the quinta to the Counts of Junqueira, whose heirs sold it at public auction, and in 1918 another family arrived, beginning five generations at Alorna by the house's account. For its three hundredth year the estate made a wine named 1723. For a sommelier, the Marquesa de Alorna is the Tejo told through a noble house: an oak aged red of the river's left bank that keeps its grapes to itself.

The house's history page gives 1723, the first name Quinta de Vale de Nabais, the naming after the conquest of Alorna, the poet Leonor (1750 to 1839, also on Wikipedia), the sale by two of her daughters to the Counts of Junqueira and the auction; 1918 and the five generations rest on that page and a Meininger company profile; Wikipedia's page on the poet tells it otherwise, the family moving to Vale de Nabais and renaming it after Pombal destroyed its palaces, which the record does not follow.

Pedro Miguel de Almeida Portugal's dates (1688 to 1756), the viceroyalty from 1744, the siege of 1746 and the title of 1748 rest on Infopedia and Wikipedia; Infopedia ends the viceroyalty in 1752 and Wikipedia in 1750, so the story gives only its start.

The red's grapes are left as the house's secret blend: one merchant (Firstleaf) lists Touriga Nacional, Touriga Franca, Castelão, Alicante Bouschet and Trincadeira and the house's own portfolio tag reads single grape, so neither is printed; the fermentation was found nowhere and is left out.

Fourteen months in barrel is the house's; new French oak and the year in bottle are Continente's sheet, and the house's 2021 page gives two years in bottle; the glass rests on Continente and Vinha's notes, the body and tannin on Firstleaf.

The appellation field says only Tejo: Continente lists the red as DOC do Tejo while a critic's tasting database lists the 2015 as IGP Tejo; the Campo and Charneca in sites are the house's Property page, and the Reserva of the two grapes is the CVR Tejo's sheet.

wine.grapes: Castelão, Alicante Bouschet, Touriga Nacional and Cabernet Sauvignon, with Petit Verdot in some vintages, by the house's sheets.
wine.sites: The family's vineyards at Almeirim, on flat, sandy ground on the left bank of the Tejo, from vines of about twenty to fifty years, by the house's sheet.
wine.making: Fermented in temperature controlled cement tanks, then aged for about thirteen months in French oak barrels, half of them new and half in their second or third use, and given time in bottle before release, by the house's sheets.
wine.glass: Blackcurrant and prune with a light floral lift, then toast, vanilla and mocha from the barrels; juicy and full in the mouth, with firm tannin and a long finish, as the house describes it.
wine.ageing: Firm in its first years, it rounds out in bottle, and the house says it can go on improving there for some years.

records.table: Falcoaria Tinto is the red of Quinta do Casal Branco, a family estate at Almeirim since 1775 whose land was once a royal falconry ground. Castelão and Alicante Bouschet meet Touriga Nacional and Cabernet Sauvignon in French oak, so expect blackcurrant, prune and mocha over firm tannin.
records.story: By the house's own account, the land of Quinta do Casal Branco at Almeirim was a royal hunting ground for four centuries, where Portugal's kings flew their falcons over the plain on the left bank of the Tejo, and a dovecote of the sixteenth century survives from that time. The house dates its own story to 1775, when the estate came to the family that has farmed it ever since, making wine beside its other work on the land. The Falcoaria range was named in homage to the falcon hunts, and it gathers the estate's oak aged red and its whites, an old vine Fernão Pires and a late harvest wine among them. The red joins Castelão, the Tejo's traditional red grape, with Alicante Bouschet, Touriga Nacional and Cabernet Sauvignon from flat, sandy ground, and gives it more than a year in French oak. Its label carries DOC do Tejo, the name the region's appellation took in 2010 in place of the DOC Ribatejo, first recognised in 2000. For a sommelier, Falcoaria is the Tejo of the old landed estates: a firm, oak aged red of the left bank's sand, named for the falcons once flown over it.

The royal hunting ground of four centuries, the falcon hunts, the dovecote of the sixteenth century and 1775 are the house's About page (marked a test page on its site), the naming of the range its Falcoaria page; an Agroportal article gives the four centuries and more than 250 years in the family, and Tanners and the Rota dos Vinhos do Tejo give 1775.

The making rests on the house's product page (cement tanks, sandy flat ground, vines of twenty to fifty years, 16 to 18 degrees Celsius) and the producer's sheet on the CVR Tejo's site (thirteen months in French oak, half new and half of second or third use); the CVR Tejo's article on its 2024 competition gives the same thirteen months and a year in bottle for the 2021.

Left out for want of a pinned source: the first winery of 1817 (two trade listings whose addresses could not be told apart in the results) and the first bottling in the early 1990s (one Agroportal article); the Lusitano stud, on the house's Coudelaria page and a merchant's, appears only in a question's explanation.

The plan's note is answered: the red, Falcoaria Tinto, is taught rather than a Grande Reserva; the plan and the region record call the label the house's falconry, but by the house's page it honours the royal falcon hunts held on the land.

The region record says the Tejo was called the Ribatejo until 2009: by the Diário da República the regional indication Ribatejano was renamed Tejo by Portaria 445/2009 of 27 April, and by the IVV the DO do Tejo was recognised by Portaria 140/2010 of 5 March in place of the DOC Ribatejo of 2000, so the label line says 2010.
The old vine white is Fernão Pires by the CVR Tejo's sheet, the late harvest half bottle by Prestige Wines Portugal, Terra de Lobos's blend by Tanners.
Living names met, none in the prose: the family member who has run the estate since the 1980s, named by merchants as José Lobo de Vasconcelos, for people.json.

wine.name: Marquesa de Cadaval Tinto
wine.grapes: Touriga Nacional, Trincadeira and Alicante Bouschet, by the house's sheet.
wine.sites: Vines of about fifty years on average at the Herdade de Muge, on the old soils of the Tejo's former delta on the left bank of the river.
wine.making: Each grape is fermented apart in stainless steel vats at about 26 degrees Celsius, with a maceration of about three weeks; the malolactic fermentation takes place in new French oak barrels, where the wine then ages for sixteen months, followed by a year in bottle before release, by the house's sheet.
wine.glass: Intense and layered, with violet from the Touriga Nacional over ripe, black fruited depth and a lift of fresh spice; full bodied, with the firm, robust frame the Trincadeira gives.
wine.ageing: Released after more than two years in barrel and bottle, it is open on release and keeps for several years more in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle an hour ahead; a large red wine glass.

records.table: Marquesa de Cadaval is the flagship red of Casa Cadaval, the ducal estate at Muge on the Tejo's left bank: Touriga Nacional, Trincadeira and Alicante Bouschet from old vines, sixteen months in new French oak. Expect violet and ripe, dark depth, and decant it for roast meats.
records.story: The Herdade de Muge, on the left bank of the Tejo, has a history older than the Cadavals' own: by the house's history a Portuguese queen lived in its palace until 1530, and in the seventeenth century the estate, then held by the Counts of Odemira, passed to the Casa Cadaval when a daughter of that house married into it. In 1648 the Crown created the title of Duke of Cadaval, and the house dates its stud of Lusitano horses to the same year. In 1926 the Marquis of Cadaval married a noblewoman of an old European family devoted to music, and in 1929 the couple settled in Portugal, at Colares near Sintra. As the Marquesa de Cadaval she became a patron of musicians, the Sintra festival among the chief beneficiaries, it is said, and she helped to recover the family's heritage at Muge; she died in 1996 and lies in the family mausoleum there. The house's flagship red bears her title. By its own account women have run the estate for five generations. For a sommelier, the Marquesa de Cadaval is a Tejo red of old vines and long oak from one of Portugal's ducal houses.

The marquise is described rather than named: the house and Visit Lisboa name her, but her year of birth was found in no source read, so she does not carry her dates; the queen and the daughter of Odemira are described for the same reason.

The grapes, the 26 degrees, the three weeks, the malolactic in new French oak, sixteen months and a year in bottle and the fifty year old vines are the house's sheet for the 2015; a critic's database gives the 2007 the same three grapes, and the former delta soils are the house's history page.

The glass rests on Cave Lusa (black fruit, violet, fresh spice) and Radar Wine (Touriga Nacional's violet, Trincadeira's structure); the serving temperature on Continente and Wine from Portugal; the Reserva in others is the house's sheet, the Trincadeira Preta a Wine House Portugal listing.

wine.name: Grande Escolha Alfrocheiro
wine.sites: Small plots of the estate beside Alpiarça, on the left bank of the Tejo across the river from Santarém; the house names no single parcel.
wine.making: By the house's account of its Alfrocheiro, picked by hand into boxes, given three days of maceration before fermentation, then fermented at about 24 degrees Celsius in open stainless steel vats and pressed in a hydraulic press; the malolactic fermentation and ten to twelve months follow in French oak barrels, new or a year old. Merchants give the Grande Escolha twelve months in barrique.
wine.glass: Deep garnet, with tobacco leaf and a warm, spiced edge over ripe, black fruited depth; deep and long in the mouth, with elegant, silky tannin.
wine.ageing: Made only in strong years and released with some time in bottle, it is open young, and a good vintage rewards a few years more.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius, as the house advises; decant a young bottle an hour ahead; a large red wine glass.

records.table: Grande Escolha Alfrocheiro is the single grape red of Quinta da Lagoalva de Cima, an Alpiarça estate that passed to the house of Palmela in 1846. Made only in strong years and aged in French oak, it shows tobacco over ripe, black fruited depth: pour it with roast meats.
records.story: Quinta da Lagoalva de Cima lies on the left bank of the Tejo beside Alpiarça, across the river from Santarém. By the house's own history the estate was bought in 1834 by the family of the Counts of Póvoa, and between 1841 and 1842 the whole of its property passed to the family's heiress, who in 1846 married the second Duke of Palmela. From then on Lagoalva belonged to the house of Palmela, and it passed down among her descendants. For its Grande Escolha reds the house bottled grapes on their own: a selection made only in strong years, it came as a Syrah and as an Alfrocheiro, a Portuguese red grape. The house's own pages have since named its single grape Alfrocheiro Grande Reserva, and it has added an organic bottling of it. By the house's account the grapes are picked by hand into small boxes and reach the cellar in the morning, then go to open steel vats, a hydraulic press and French oak, new or a year old, for the malolactic fermentation and the ageing. For a sommelier, the Grande Escolha shows a Portuguese grape standing alone on the Tejo's left bank, from an estate whose history runs through one of the country's noble houses.

records.table: 1836 Grande Reserva is the red of the Companhia das Lezírias, the farm company of the Tejo's floodplain formed in 1836: Alicante Bouschet alone from the Catapereiro sand, fermented in a lagar and aged eighteen months in French oak. Decant it for roast meats or cured sausages.
records.story: The Companhia das Lezírias was formed in June 1836, when the Crown sold lands near Lisbon to a group of investors: the lezírias, the flood meadows of the lower Tejo, with the heaths of the Charneca beyond them, by the company's own account reaching from the Tejo to the Sado. Wine came later. By its history the first vineyard was planted in 1881, on the sandy Charneca at Catapereiro, where its winery stands. After the revolution of 1974 the company was nationalised, in 1975 by its own account, and in 1989 a decree law made it a public limited company of wholly public capital. Its Grande Reserva range takes the year of the founding as its name, 1836, and in the company's own words honours the men and women who since then have made it what it is. The red is Alicante Bouschet alone, an inky grape with red flesh, from the Catapereiro sand, fermented in a lagar with its own yeasts and given a year and a half in French oak. Beside it the Tyto Alba range is named for the barn owl, which the company honours as a sign of its land's environmental health. For a sommelier, 1836 is the Charneca's dark, firm red: a single grape from sand, made in a lagar, by a company older than its vines.

others.note: A range named for the barn owl, which the company honours as a sign of its land's environmental health.

traps: The 1836 on the label is the year the company was formed, not a vintage: its first vineyard was planted only in 1881.
The 1836 Grande Reserva red is Alicante Bouschet alone, a grape with red flesh, not a blend of the Tejo's Castelão and Trincadeira.

cards.front: Companhia das Lezírias 1836 Grande Reserva red: which grape, and how long in oak?
cards.back: Alicante Bouschet alone, eighteen months in French oak barrels, half new and half in their second use.

cards.front: When did the Companhia das Lezírias plant its first vineyard, and where?
cards.back: In 1881, on the sandy Charneca at Catapereiro, forty five years after the company was formed.

questions.q: A guest asks how the Companhia das Lezírias ferments its 1836 Grande Reserva red. Which answer fits?
opts: In a lagar with its own yeasts
In large oak vats with bought yeasts
In clay amphorae set in sand
questions.exp: The company ferments it with its own yeasts in a lagar at about 25 degrees Celsius with a daily punch down, then ages it eighteen months in French oak; no amphora or egg is used.

questions.q: The Grande Reserva range of the Companhia das Lezírias is called 1836. What does the year mark?
opts: The planting of its first vineyard
questions.exp: The company was formed in June 1836, when the Crown sold lands near Lisbon; its first vineyard came only in 1881 and its nationalisation in 1975.

report: Searches for this record: 4 of the group's share of 35, two on the company's own domains; no fetch tried.

June 1836 and the Crown's sale of lands near Lisbon are the company's history page, Wikipedia and the CVR Tejo's guide; the investors and the reach from the Tejo to the Sado are the company's and Wikipedia's; the first vineyard of 1881 at Catapereiro is the company's history page and the CVR Tejo's guide.

Nationalisation is 1975 on the company's presentation page, while its horse stud's history page dates it to 25 April 1974 and Wikipedia's after 138 years points to 1974, so the story says after the revolution of 1974, in 1975 by its own account; 1989 and the public limited company are its statutes page (Decree Law 182/89).

The red's making, grape, sand and climate are the company's page for the 2016 and the CVR Tejo's sheet for the 2015, which also gives the homage to the men and women since 1836; the old vines a CVR Tejo text gives the red are found on the company's own pages only for the white, so the red's vine age is left out.
The plan's note is answered: the 1836 range is made red and white, and the red is taught as the company's page sets the range; the white is in others.
The Tyto Alba name and its owl are a company document on the Tyto Alba wines and a bird watching site; the plan's vines in the estuary's nature reserve were not found, so they are not in the record.
The glass and the serving temperature are the company's own page; the region record's Catapereiro on the Charneca sand is borne out.
No living person is named or was met by name.
